newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Internet rules not meant to choke debate - Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Internet rules not meant to choke debate - Singapore.

text.p: The Singapore government said on Thursday that measures to regulate political content on the Internet were not aimed at curtailing political discussion.
"It's not our intention at all to curtail political discussion on the Internet," Mohamed Maidin, Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministry of Information and the Arts, told parliament.

Nominated member of parliament Walter Woon had asked for an explanation of a clause in the Internet content guidelines which says the government would not allow any matter that "tends to bring the Government into hatred or contempt, or which excites disaffection against the government".
Maidin said the guidelines helped set a minimum standard of conduct and community values relating to public morals, racial and religious harmony, and public security and national defence.

He said the clause cited by Woon came under the area of public security and national defence and was based on the Sedition Act. This Act seeks to outlaw any seditious action, speech, words or publication.

"But some parts of the Sedition Act allow for exceptions to be made where the intentions are good and they found that something is necessary to be debated for the good of Singapore," Maidin said. "If the intention is good, the government will not stop such discussions."
Asked by Woon to confirm that Singaporeans were entitled to disagree with the government and could express their disagreement freely on the Internet, Maidin said: "I say yes."
Maidin added his ministry would continue to improve the regulations, whether that involved tightening or easing them.

Singapore government measures to regulate political and religious content on the Internet and keep it free of pornography became effective from July 15. They require all Internet service operators and local content providers to be registered with the Singapore Broadcasting Authority (SBA). Failure to heed the guidelines can result in an unspecified fine or cancellation of the licence.
The SBA had said the guidelines were broad but that did not mean criticism of the government was not allowed, as long as it was done responsibly.
